body:
The first rain to run off a roof carries whatever has settled there since the last storm. The CDC excerpt used for this entry says that includes accumulated dust, leaves and animal feces. A first-flush diverter holds back this early water so it does not flow into the storage cistern.

The mechanism described is a vertical pipe, or standpipe, connected to the roof runoff line ahead of the cistern. The source says it collects the initial 1 to 2 mm of roof runoff. Inside the pipe sits a floating plastic ball. As the standpipe fills, the ball rises with the water until it seals against a gasket seat at the top. With that path closed, later runoff, which the source describes as cleaner, continues on into the primary storage cistern.

To size the standpipe, multiply the roof's catchment area by the depth you want to discard: each millimeter of rain over one square meter of roof is one liter of water. A 50 square meter roof and a 2 mm first flush therefore call for a pipe holding about 100 liters.

This entry covers only how diversion works. The source excerpt does not say how to empty the standpipe between storms or whether stored rainwater is safe to drink, so it makes no claim about either.

review.scope: Source consistency check: verifies that the entry's factual statements about first-flush diversion (the contaminants removed, the 1 to 2 mm diversion depth, and the standpipe with its floating ball and gasket seal) reflect the provided CDC source excerpt, that attribution is accurate, and that limitations are declared. The liter-per-square-meter sizing arithmetic is a unit conversion, not a claim from the source. The excerpt's figure of 10 to 20 gallons per 1,000 square feet is left out because it does not match the 1 to 2 mm depth, which works out to about 25 to 49 gallons. Not independent laboratory, engineering or water-safety verification.

sources.title: CDC — Rainwater Collection and First-Flush Diversion

summary: A first-flush diverter catches the first 1 to 2 mm of roof runoff, which carries dust, leaves and animal feces, in a vertical pipe. When the pipe fills, a floating ball seals it, and the later, cleaner runoff flows on to the storage cistern.
title: Send the dirtiest rain away from the tank
